$comment: §4.1c mutation coverage for every rendered VERDICT and every rendered
MEASUREMENT in this lab. One entry per marker, of either family: a
data-verdict marker says what happened, a data-claim marker is a number the
reader is invited to check, and a number painted with no mutation behind it
is exactly as unchecked as a verdict painted with none.
A mutation counts as a KILL only when the unmutated baseline PASSED in the
same run, the failure is that marker's OWN assertion (not a build error, a
blank page, a timeout, or the whole suite going red), and the run served the
mutated code. mutations/run.mjs enforces all three; it runs with CI=1 so
playwright.config.ts's reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI is false and no
stale server on port 4667 can answer for an unmutated checkout.
e2e/verdicts.spec.ts fails if the page renders a marker of either family
that this file does not cover, fails if this file claims a marker the page
never renders, and fails if a recorded kill's test does not go through the
shared helpers (expectVerdict / expectNoVerdict / readClaim) — a spec that
merely mentions a marker id is not a spec that asserts it. A marker
reachable only on a failure path carries rendersOnlyUnderMutation: true, and
the spec then requires it to be ABSENT from the healthy page, so the flag
cannot be used to hide a verdict that really does render.
D6: 'goes through the shared helper' is judged at RUNTIME, not by reading
spec source. Each helper writes the (test title, marker id) pair it actually
EXECUTES to a run-scoped sink, and e2e/global-teardown.ts fails the run when
a record's pair never appeared. A commented-out call leaves text and no
line; a call moved to another test of the same file appears under another
title. Neither satisfies the rule any more.
asserts: the (text, state) pairs the killing test must pass to expectVerdict
for that marker, IN ORDER - every one of them, and nothing else. Recording
the pair proves the helper ran; it cannot tell a real expectation from one
the test read off the page a line earlier, because both execute. The pin
makes the argument come from somewhere other than the marker under test, so
a page-derived argument becomes the MUTATED text under the recorded
mutation, stops matching, and fails inside the marker's own test. Order
rather than membership: a killing test that walks two branches hands over
two pairs, and under a mutation that merely SWAPS the branches a
page-derived argument hands back the same two pairs the other way round,
which a set comparison cannot see. Verdict records
only: a data-claim oracle's expectation is recomputed from the run (a Wilson
interval, an exact collision probability) and there is no honest literal to
pin, so a tautological CLAIM oracle is caught by the mutation sweep rather
than by the coverage rule. That limit is stated in README.md rather than
left to be discovered.

mutations.grep: the switching rows claim matches the bound recomputed at the chosen n
mutations.why: Measures the FIRST q point and copies it into every later row, correcting only the columns a row-local oracle would notice: queries, bound, and the within-tolerance flag derived from them. Every row then satisfies its own internal consistency by construction — measured IS the Wilson estimate of its own wins/trials, because it is the same row — while the caption above still reads "N q values, M trials each" and the exhibit still teaches advantage rising with q. This is the shape the 2026-09-21 audit found alive at 35/35 green: the oracle checked each row against itself and nothing bound a row to its own run. It is killed by comparing each row's measured advantage with the per-q prediction exactFunctionCollisionProbability(n, q) recomputed in the spec, within that row's own rendered tolerance.
mutations.scope: Deliberately leaves the trial ledgers alone: the auditor confirmed those are genuine per-trial sums by mutating src/game/challenger.ts so one trial stops contributing, which kills. The defect this records is in what the CURVE binds together, not in how a point is counted.
